public_rationale: Hayabusa Research's October 25, 2026 assessment said broad cross-industry contagion was not established [e1]. This assessment does not establish the broad investment collapse required to test whether that collapse itself makes comparable AI compute materially cheaper [e1].
limitations: The collapse condition remains unverified. This does not prove that no collapse occurred.
The packet contains no qualifying comparison of compute costs before and after a collapse.
Supplier operating costs and customer service prices require separate comparisons that account for hardware, performance, service quality and contract terms.
The forecast has no deadline or numerical threshold for a material reduction.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: AI compute is not going to become magically cheaper once the bubble bursts.

statement.excerpt: This shit isn’t going to become magically cheaper once the bubble bursts, and considering the demand doesn’t appear to be there at scale with two-thirds of all venture capital funding focused on AI, I’m not sure what people expect to happen.

from_speaker: isn’t going to become magically cheaper
our_interpretation: This shit refers to supplying and using AI compute in the surrounding discussion.
Magically is rhetorical emphasis, not a literal supernatural condition. The plain reading is that a collapse will not itself produce a material reduction in comparable compute costs.
The antecedent is a broad AI investment collapse affecting the infrastructure market described in the post.
Supplier operating costs and customer compute-service prices must be examined separately.
No company-specific financial amount or accounting measure is asserted, so metric_scope is null.
criteria.support_condition: After an established collapse, comparable operating-cost and service-price evidence shows no material collapse-driven reduction. A limited period without a reduction provides only provisional support for this undated negative.
criteria.contradiction_condition: After an established collapse, like-for-like operating costs or compute-service prices fall materially, with evidence connecting the reduction to the collapse rather than unrelated technological progress or changed service quality.
